rules.summary: Gameplay logic must not live in React components or canvas rendering code, and renderer or UI-only objects must never become gameplay or save state.
Important design values must live in structured content and documented tool workflows instead of scattered runtime constants.

Keep `content/source`, `content/generated`, `content/authored`, and runtime bundles as separate layers; source imports stay immutable, generated outputs change intentionally through regeneration or documented pipeline work, and authored data owns project-specific tuning.
Keep the player game and internal studio as separate apps that share contracts, schemas, and helpers through packages instead of duplicating logic.
Static-first hosting and local-only save assumptions remain active until an explicit backend or cloud-save architecture decision updates the canonical docs.
Guideline files remain English-only, and archive docs remain historical context rather than active implementation guidance.
Documentation precedence is `AGENTS.md`, then active normative docs in `docs/ai/`, then active task-specific normative docs, then active reference docs, and finally archive docs.
Every tracked guideline markdown file in the active documentation set must declare `doc-meta` status and scope.
Every normative bullet in an active normative doc must carry exactly one inline rule marker using the `RULE:<ID>` convention rendered as `[RULE:...]`.
Every active rule ID must appear exactly once in [rule-registry.json](./rule-registry.json) and must name a single canonical home.

Adding, changing, relocating, or removing active rules requires same-change updates to the canonical doc and [rule-registry.json](./rule-registry.json); update [rule-coverage.md](./rule-coverage.md) only when its audit narrative, source coverage matrix, or canonical ownership notes become inaccurate.
Temporary decision docs must be migrated into permanent canonical docs and then removed, archived, or converted into redirect stubs.
Read [docs/ai/README.md](./docs/ai/README.md) before any repo change.
Read the relevant normative domain docs before changing gameplay, UI, save, content, tooling, or documentation.
Do not use archive docs as the canonical source of truth; use them only to recover historical rationale.
Keep simulation, rendering, UI, platform, save, and content responsibilities separated; simulation remains the gameplay source of truth.

Keep player-facing text bilingual, store text-bearing source files in UTF-8, preserve accents and special characters, and update the affected canonical docs plus rule tracking when active guidance changes.

Keep [docs/product/todo-system.md](./docs/product/todo-system.md) and [docs/product/todo-backlog.md](./docs/product/todo-backlog.md) as the canonical tracked-work system, and update them when accepted scope or completion status changes.
Documentation changes do not pass review until `node scripts/validate-docs.mjs` succeeds.
Save-model or runtime-state changes require deterministic tests for reconstruction, migrations, and affected progression behavior.
Content or schema changes require schema validation plus cross-reference validation for authored data and registry exposure.
UI changes require responsive and localization review, and browser or Playwright coverage only when the change is visually or interaction-wise risky.
Broken active links, missing rule IDs, orphan normative docs, or active rules that exist only in archive placement are hard validation failures.
Start every change by reading [README.md](./README.md) plus the relevant normative domain docs before making design or implementation decisions.
Choose the safest edit surface in this order: tool workflow or authored data, then schemas or overrides, then generators, and only then runtime code.
When runtime contracts, save shapes, or content schemas change, update the affected docs, tests, and migrations in the same change set.
When UI changes land, preserve the deliberate split between desktop landscape and mobile portrait layouts and keep localization intact.
Run `node scripts/validate-docs.mjs` for documentation or rule changes, and run the matching package checks from the matrix below for runtime, schema, content, tooling, or UI changes.
Use browser or Playwright checks only when the UI change is complex, highly interactive, or visually risky; simple nonvisual edits do not require them.

Treat ambiguity as a hard blocker for code, project, and documentation work when it affects the real goal, touched scope, expected result, change aggressiveness, or leaves multiple materially different valid interpretations; stop before additional writes when that ambiguity appears.

When ambiguity blocks execution, ask one short clarification using this exact format on separate lines: `BLOCKER`, `Question: <one short, simple question>`, `Options:`, `- <option 1>`, `- <option 2>`, optional third option only if needed, `Recommended: <clear recommendation>`, `Impact: <short explanation of the consequences of each direction>`.

Use the blocker format only for genuinely blocking project ambiguity; do not use it for trivial non-project requests or when one execution direction is already clear from the active docs and user context.

When accepted work is added, completed, deferred, split, or reprioritized, update [../product/todo-backlog.md](../product/todo-backlog.md) in the same change set, and update [../product/todo-system.md](../product/todo-system.md) if the tracking workflow itself changes.

`content/source` stores raw imported source payloads, `content/generated` stores normalized generated outputs, `content/authored` stores project-authored gameplay data, and runtime bundles store shipped production groupings.

Canonical imported source data is never hand-edited; generated data changes through regeneration or explicitly documented pipeline work, authored data owns project-specific tuning and references, and Pokemon visual fields in generated data use the Platinum front sprite source rather than official artwork.
Authored content must validate against shared schemas and cross-document references before exposure to apps.
Consumers use the typed content registry instead of ad hoc direct JSON imports.
New content domains require schema coverage, registry validation, docs, and ownership declarations before they join the workflow.

`contracts` owns portable domain types, `content-schema` owns validation schemas, `content-data` owns typed registry and cross-reference validation, `game-core` owns simulation and save helpers, and apps own presentation and bootstrapping.
Dependency direction flows from apps into shared packages; gameplay packages must not import app-specific UI code.
New systems must declare their owning layer and allowed dependencies before implementation starts.
Shared schemas, helpers, and visual tokens belong in shared packages instead of being duplicated across apps.
Avoid monolithic or mixed-responsibility modules; keep files and modules intentionally scoped by domain.
Simulation is the gameplay source of truth; render only draws, UI presents and dispatches intent, and platform owns lifecycle, layout, language, and persistence plumbing.
Important gameplay rules must not depend on active-tab cadence, render loops, or browser background timer behavior.
Combat stepping must remain deterministic from timestamps and saved session state.
Type logic, reaction resolution, stat derivation, progression state, and battle flow belong to `game-core` or equivalent runtime layers rather than React or canvas code.
Wild, boss, trainer, and gym flows remain explicit runtime paths instead of UI-only branches.

Combat animation and VFX cues are transient presentation events derived from resolved runtime attacks, are never persisted in save state, and must not replay offline catch-up as if it were live action.
V1 save is local-first with IndexedDB primary storage, manual export or import, reset support, and rotating local backups.
Keep active state in memory, batch noisy writes, and flush on critical progression events plus page-hide or visibility-risk moments.
Save data persists progression-critical domains including species or team state, quests, zones, flags, dialogue state, combat sessions, counters, and currency.
Every save shape change ships with deterministic migration logic and targeted tests.
Save data never stores renderer objects or UI-only state, and battle snapshots must keep the data required for deterministic reconstruction.
Combat resolves through ordered team slots around a single current enemy, and empty slots still consume action windows.
Slot order, typing, reactions, talents, and battle-level modifiers are first-class combat dimensions and must remain legible in the UI.
Type and reaction resolution are deterministic runtime systems rather than presentation-only effects.
Zone, boss or event, trainer, and gym fights are distinct supported combat modes, with gym battles built on trainer-battle rules.
Captures unlock usable species instead of persistent individual units, and newly unlocked species always start at level 1.
Capturing an evolved form unlocks the stage-1 species, and evolution unlocks the next species at level 1 as a prestige-like reinvestment path.
Per-family capture mastery, per-species counters, quests, flags, and zone completion are persistent progression systems.
Main quests drive progression and side quests drive optional rewards, but both use one core quest framework and may gate zones, NPC states, and systems.
Offensive typing defaults, asymmetrical combat stats, cosmetic-only shiny or skin systems, and explicit rank or tuning data remain documented systems rather than hidden hardcoded exceptions.

Team composition forbids duplicate species, forbids multiple members of the same evolution family except the Eevee family, and evolution targets can unlock only once; when evolution runtime replaces a species, the evolved form must take the same team slot automatically.
Each species has at most one fixed passive talent, and the player does not manually choose talents.
Talents hook into explicit documented phases such as battle start, slot turn start, attack resolution, damage, enemy defeat or spawn, and stat or presentation derivation.
Talent stacking, targeting, sequence effects, and priority must be deterministic and documented.
Simple or common talents may be data-backed, but advanced behavior stays code-backed behind stable hooks instead of ad hoc exceptions.
Adding or changing a talent requires docs, tests, and an explicit choice of data-backed, code-backed, or hybrid ownership.
Zones are typed nodes in a world graph; combat and pacifist zones share a common framework but do not share identical behavior assumptions.
Visibility, accessibility, completion, adjacency, conditional unlocks, and backtracking are data-driven progression state and must be saved.
Pacifist zones support structured activities such as dialogue, team management, gym entry, NPC unlocks, and future services without combat assumptions.
Zone events, bosses, trainer battles, and gym battles are first-class systems implemented through explicit data and runtime handlers rather than bespoke one-offs.
Battle entry constraints, timers, maluses, unlock effects, and locked reasons must be validated before start and made legible in the UI or world map.
All player-facing text must support both English and French from the start.
English is the fallback locale, and French auto-selection may follow browser or device language detection in the runtime layer.
Single-language gameplay or UI text is forbidden in active player-facing flows; localized content belongs in localized data structures.
Text-bearing source files must stay UTF-8, preserve accents and special characters, and treat missing translations as validation debt with safe fallback to English.
Prioritize tests that protect docs and architecture contracts, content validation, save or migration safety, deterministic combat, progression, responsive layout, and localization fallback.
Elapsed-time reconstruction coverage must include hidden tabs, minimized windows, device sleep, and long offline gaps.
Content validation must catch invalid links, missing localized strings, and broken quest, battle, dialogue, or species references.
Browser or Playwright checks are required only for complex, interactive, or visually risky UI changes; simple nonvisual changes do not require them.
Important design values belong in structured editable data and dedicated tools rather than scattered engine constants.

Safe manual edit surfaces are authored data and documented override files; source imports are immutable and generated outputs are regenerated artifacts unless the change explicitly targets the generator pipeline.
Editable data must stay human-readable, shallow, validated, and documented when fields control balance or visuals.
Tool-first editing is the default for normal content and tuning changes; direct file edits are acceptable only when tool coverage is missing or implementation work is required.
New editable domains must define schema coverage, validation, defaults or reset strategy, docs, and ownership before they join the workflow.
UI must stay compact, colorful, flat, simple, and fast to scan; filler text and redundant chrome are forbidden.
Always-on gameplay uses compact HUD surfaces, while deep interactions use larger focus windows in the project PC-window language.
Desktop landscape and mobile portrait are distinct intentional layouts rather than shrink-only variants.
Every visible label must justify its footprint; prefer grouping, hierarchy, icons, and state cues before explanatory text.

Visual styling uses restrained flat surfaces, disciplined spacing, readable color coding, minimal decorative clutter, Platinum front sprites for Pokemon representations, and distinct desktop-ring versus mobile-arc battle staging while staying consistent with the Pokemon-adjacent direction.

Battle presentation keeps a constant attack rhythm across physical and special attacks, uses local renderer-owned transient VFX only, and may reduce mobile effect budgets without changing gameplay timing.
